title: Relative Flatness and Generalization
publication_status_observed: NeurIPS 2021 (arXiv:2001.00939v4, under review at time of first arXiv submission 2020)
main_claims: Flatness explains generalization only when data is 'representative' and feature labels are approximately locally constant in feature space.

A novel relative flatness measure—defined via the loss Hessian relative to parameter norms—is invariant to linear reparameterizations of ReLU networks, resolving Dinh et al.'s reparameterization critique.
Relative flatness correlates more strongly with generalization than existing flatness measures (trace of Hessian, Fisher-Rao norm) on CIFAR-10.
methodology: The generalization gap is decomposed into a representativeness term and a feature robustness term using density estimation in feature space. Feature robustness is connected to the loss Hessian via a key identity relating multiplicative feature perturbations to parameter perturbations. A relative flatness measure is derived that simplifies to ridge regression for ordinary least squares. Empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10 compares the relative flatness measure against other flatness measures for correlation with generalization gap. Both theoretical derivations and synthetic experiments are used.
key_results: Relative flatness outperforms state-of-the-art flatness measures in correlation with generalization on CIFAR-10.
The connection between flatness and generalization holds specifically when labels are approximately locally constant in feature space—a condition satisfied by most natural image classification tasks.
The relative flatness measure simplifies to ridge/Tikhonov regularization for ordinary least squares, providing a clean theoretical link.
limitations: The theoretical analysis assumes a noise-free setting where each input has a unique label, which may not hold for noisy real-world datasets.
The generalization bound depends on feature dimensionality, which can be large for deep networks, potentially making the bound vacuous.
Empirical validation is limited to CIFAR-10; behavior on larger datasets or under distribution shift is not evaluated.
relevance_to_rq: Relevant to the flatness_theory sub-topic: provides rigorous conditions under which flatness predicts generalization and introduces a reparameterization-invariant flatness measure. Directly addresses the Dinh et al. counter-argument that flatness measures are scale-dependent, which is important background for interpreting sharpness comparisons between SAM and SWA.
